danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 10
paragraphs: Fyrst Andrej tog ophold i Brünn hos Bilibin, en russisk bekendt i den diplomatiske tjeneste.

»Ah, min kære fyrste! Jeg kunne ikke have fået en mere velkommen gæst,« sagde Bilibin, da han kom ud for at tage imod fyrst Andrej. »Franz, læg fyrstens ting i mit soveværelse,« sagde han til tjeneren, der førte Bolkonskij ind. »Så du er en sejrskuré? Pragtfuldt! Og jeg sidder her og er syg, som du kan se.«

Efter at have vasket sig og klædt sig om kom fyrst Andrej ind i diplomatens luksuriøse arbejdsværelse og satte sig til det middagsmåltid, der var gjort klar til ham. Bilibin lænede sig behageligt tilbage ved kaminen.

Efter sin rejse og det felttog, hvor han havde været berøvet al renligheds bekvemmelighed og alle livets forfinelser, følte fyrst Andrej en behagelig hvile midt i luksuriøse omgivelser som dem, han var vant til fra barndommen. Desuden var det rart, efter sin modtagelse hos østrigerne, at tale — om ikke på russisk (for de talte fransk) — så i det mindste med en russer, der, mente han, delte den almindelige russiske antipati mod østrigerne, som var særlig stærk på det tidspunkt.

Bilibin var en femogtyveårig mand, ungkarl og af samme kreds som fyrst Andrej. De havde kendt hinanden i forvejen i Petersborg, men var kommet hinanden nærmere, da fyrst Andrej var i Wien med Kutuzov. Ligesom fyrst Andrej var en ung mand, der lovede at nå højt i den militære profession, lovede Bilibin i endnu højere grad det samme i den diplomatiske karriere. Han var stadig en ung mand, men ikke længere en ung diplomat, da han var trådt i tjeneste som seksten-årig, havde været i Paris og København og nu beklædte en temmelig vigtig post i Wien. Både udenrigsministeren og vores ambassadør i Wien kendte og satte pris på ham. Han var ikke en af de mange diplomater, der er agtede, fordi de har visse negative egenskaber, undgår at gøre visse ting og taler fransk. Han var en af dem, der holder af at arbejde, forstår at gøre det, og trods sin dovenskab somme tider tilbragte en hel nat ved sit skrivebord. Han arbejdede godt, uanset arbejdets vigtighed. Det var ikke spørgsmålet »hvad for?« men spørgsmålet »hvordan?« der interesserede ham. Hvad den diplomatiske sag end drejede sig om, var det ham ligegyldigt, men det var ham en stor fornøjelse at udarbejde et cirkulære, et memorandum eller en rapport dygtigt, præcist og elegant. Bilibins tjenester blev værdsat ikke blot for det, han skrev, men også for hans dygtighed i omgang og samtale med de højeste kredse.

Bilibin holdt af samtale, ligesom han holdt af arbejde, kun når den kunne gøres elegant og vittig. I selskab ventede han altid på en lejlighed til at sige noget slående og deltog kun i en samtale, når det var muligt. Hans tale var altid krydret med vittigt originale, afrundede vendinger af almen interesse. Disse bonmot'er blev forberedt i hans hjerneværksted i en transportabel form, som om det var med vilje, så ubetydelige selskabsmennesker kunne bære dem fra salon til salon. Og faktisk gik Bilibins vittigheder fra mund til mund i de wienske saloner og havde ofte indflydelse på sager, der blev anset for vigtige.

Hans tynde, slidte, gustne ansigt var dækket af dybe rynker, der altid så rene og velskurede ud som fingerspidserne efter et russisk dampbad. Bevægelsen af disse rynker udgjorde det vigtigste mimiske spil i hans ansigt. Snart trak panden sig sammen i dybe folder, og øjenbrynene hævedes; snart sænkede øjenbrynene sig, og dybe rynker krusede kinderne. Hans små, dybtliggende øjne glimtede altid og kiggede lige ud.
»Nå, fortæl mig om dine bedrifter,« sagde han.
Bolkonskij fortalte meget beskedent, uden nogensinde at nævne sig selv, om slaget og om sin modtagelse hos krigsministeren.
»De modtog mig og mine nyheder, som man modtager en hund i keglespil,« sagde han afslutningsvis.
Bilibin smilede, og rynkerne i hans ansigt forsvandt.

»Cependant, mon cher,« bemærkede han, idet han betragtede sine negle på afstand og rynkede huden over venstre øje, »malgré la haute estime que je professe pour den ortodokse russiske hær, j’avoue que votre victoire n’est pas des plus victorieuses.« *
* »Men, kære ven, med al min agtelse for den ortodokse russiske hær må jeg sige, at Deres sejr ikke var særlig sejrrig.«
Han fortsatte med at tale på denne måde på fransk og kun bruge russiske ord, når han ønskede at lægge foragtelig vægt på noget.
»Jamen altså! I falder med alle jeres styrker over den stakkels Mortier og hans ene division, og alligevel slipper Mortier gennem fingrene! Hvor er sejren?«
»Men alvorligt talt,« sagde fyrst Andrej, »vi kan dog i det mindste sige uden at prale, at det var lidt bedre end ved Ulm ...«
»Hvorfor tog I ikke en eneste marskal til fange for os?«
»Fordi ikke alting går, som man venter, eller med en parades glathed. Vi havde som sagt ventet at nå deres ryg klokken syv om morgenen, men nåede den ikke før klokken fem om eftermiddagen.«
»Og hvorfor gjorde I det ikke klokken syv? I burde have været der klokken syv,« svarede Bilibin med et smil. »I burde have været der klokken syv.«
»Hvorfor lykkedes det Dem ikke ad diplomatisk vej at overbevise Bonaparte om, at han hellere skulle lade Genova i fred?« replicerede fyrst Andrej i samme toneleje.

»Jeg ved det,« afbrød Bilibin, »du tænker, at det er nemt at tage marskaller til fange, når man sidder i en sofa ved kaminen! Det er sandt, men alligevel — hvorfor tog I ham ikke? Så bliv ikke overrasket, hvis ikke kun krigsministeren, men også Hans Allerhelligste Majestæt, kejser og konge Franz, er ubetinget begejstret for jeres sejr. Selv jeg, en fattig sekretær ved den russiske ambassade, føler ikke noget behov for i min glædes tegn at give min Franz en thaler eller lade ham gå med sin Liebchen til Prateren ... Ganske vist har vi ingen Prater her ...«
Han kiggede lige på fyrst Andrej og glattede pludselig sin panderynke.

»Nu er det min tur til at spørge dig 'hvorfor?', mon cher,« sagde Bolkonskij. »Jeg indrømmer, at jeg ikke forstår; måske er der diplomatiske finheder her, der overgår min ringe forstand, men jeg kan ikke gennemskue det. Mack mister en hel hær, ærkehertug Ferdinand og ærkehertug Karl giver ikke livstegn fra sig og begår den ene brøler efter den anden. Kutuzov alene vinder en ægte sejr, bryder fortryllelsen af franskmændenes uovervindelighed, og krigsministeren gider ikke engang høre detaljerne.«

»Det er netop det, min kære ven. Ser du, det hedder hurra for zaren, for Rusland, for den ortodokse tro! Alt det er smukt, men hvad bekymrer vi os — det vil sige det østrigske hof — om jeres sejre? Bring os pæne nyheder om en sejr vundet af ærkehertug Karl eller Ferdinand (den ene ærkehertug er lige så god som den anden, det ved du), og om det så blot er over et brandkorps af Bonapartes, det ville være en anden sag, og vi fyrer kanonskud af! Men den slags ting ser nærmest ud til at være gjort med vilje for at irritere os. Ærkehertug Karl gør ingenting, ærkehertug Ferdinand blamerer sig. I forlader Wien, opgiver dets forsvar — som ville I sige: 'Himlen er med os, men Himlen hjælpe jer og jeres hovedstad!' Den ene general, vi alle holdt af, Schmidt, ham udsætter I for en kugle, og så lykønsker I os med sejren! Indrøm, at mere irriterende nyheder end jeres ikke kunne udtænkes. Det er som gjort med vilje, med vilje. Og desuden, selv om I vandt en strålende sejr, om selv ærkehertug Karl vandt en sejr — hvad ville det ændre ved krigens overordnede gang? Det er for sent nu, da Wien er besat af den franske hær!«
»Hvad? Besat? Wien besat?«
»Ikke blot besat, men Bonaparte er på Schönbrunn, og greven, vores kære grev Vrbna, går til ham for at modtage ordrer.«
Efter rejsens strabadser og indtryk og især efter at have spist kunne Bolkonskij ikke fatte den fulde rækkevidde af de ord, han hørte.

»Grev Lichtenfels var her i morges,« fortsatte Bilibin, »og viste mig et brev med en fuldstændig beskrivelse af den franske parade i Wien: fyrst Murat et tout le tremblement ... Du ser, at din sejr ikke er nogen stor glæde, og at du ikke kan modtages som en frelser.«

»Det er mig virkelig ligegyldigt, fuldstændig ligegyldigt,« sagde fyrst Andrej, der begyndte at indse, at hans nyhed om slaget ved Krems virkelig var af ringe betydning i lyset af begivenheder som Østrigs hovedstads fald. »Hvordan er Wien blevet indtaget? Hvad med broen og dens berømte brohoved og fyrst Auersperg? Vi hørte, at fyrst Auersperg forsvarede Wien?«

»Fyrst Auersperg er på denne, vores side af floden, og forsvarer os — det gør han ganske vist ret dårligt, men alligevel forsvarer han os. Men Wien er på den anden side. Nej, broen er endnu ikke taget, og jeg håber, den ikke bliver det, for den er mineret, og der er givet ordre til at sprænge den i luften. Ellers ville vi for længst have været oppe i Bøhmens bjerge, og du og din hær ville have tilbragt en ubehagelig stund mellem to ildfronter.«
»Men det betyder dog ikke, at felttoget er forbi,« sagde fyrst Andrej.

»Tja, det tror jeg nok. Storhederne herude tror det også, men de tør ikke sige det. Det bliver, som jeg sagde ved felttogets begyndelse: det er ikke jeres skærmydsler ved Dürrenstein eller krudt overhovedet, der afgør sagen, men dem der udtænkte den,« sagde Bilibin og citerede et af sine egne bonmot'er, glattede sine panderynker og holdt en pause. »Det eneste spørgsmål er, hvad der kommer ud af mødet mellem kejser Alexander og den preussiske konge i Berlin. Hvis Preussen slutter sig til de allierede, tvinges Østrigs hånd, og der bliver krig. Hvis ikke, er det bare et spørgsmål om, hvor man skal udarbejde den nye Campo Formio-fred.«
»Sikken et usædvanligt geni!« udbrød fyrst Andrej pludselig og knyttede sin lille hånd og slog i bordet. »Og sikken et held den mand har!«

»Buonaparte?« sagde Bilibin spørgende og rynkede panden for at antyde, at han var ved at sige noget vittigt. »Buonaparte?« gentog han med eftertryk på u'et: »Jeg mener dog, at nu, da han dikterer love for Østrig fra Schönbrunn, il faut lui faire grâce de l'u! (vi må fritage ham for u'et!) Jeg vil bestemt følge denne nyskabelse og blot kalde ham Bonaparte!«
»Vi må fritage ham for u'et!«
»Men spøg til side,« sagde fyrst Andrej, »mener du virkelig, at felttoget er forbi?«

»Det mener jeg: Østrig er blevet gjort til grin, og det er man ikke vant til. Man vil tage revanche. Og man er blevet gjort til nar i første omgang, fordi landets provinser er blevet plyndret — de siger, at den hellige russiske hær hærger frygteligt — hæren er tilintetgjort, hovedstaden taget, og alt dette for den sardinske majestæts smukke øjnes skyld. Og derfor — dette er mellem os — fornemmer jeg instinktivt, at vi bliver bedraget, at mit instinkt fortæller mig om forhandlinger med Frankrig og planer om fred, en hemmelig fred indgået separat.«
»Smukke øjne.«
»Umuligt!« udbrød fyrst Andrej. »Det ville være for lavt.«
»Tiden vil vise,« svarede Bilibin, idet hans ansigt atter blev glat som tegn på, at samtalen var slut.

Da fyrst Andrej nåede det værelse, der var gjort klar til ham, og lagde sig i en ren skjorte på duntæppet med dets varme og duftende puder, følte han, at det slag, han havde bragt nyt om, var langt, langt borte fra ham. Alliancen med Preussen, Østrigs troløshed, Bonapartes nye triumf, morgendagens levée og parade og audiens hos kejser Franz optog hans tanker.

Han lukkede øjnene, og straks syntes kanonade, musketter og hjulraslen at fylde hans ører, og nu igen trukket ud i en tynd linje steg musketérerne ned ad bakken, franskmændene skød, og han mærkede hjertet hamre, mens han red fremad ved Schmidts side med kuglerne muntert hvinende rundt om ham, og han oplevede tidobbelt livets glæde, som han ikke havde gjort det siden barndommen.
Han vågnede ...
»Ja, alt det skete!« sagde han og smilede lykkeligt til sig selv som et barn, og faldt i en dyb, ungdommelig søvn.

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Prince Andrew stayed in Brünn with Bilíbin, a Russian he knew from the diplomatic service.

"Ah, my dear Prince! I couldn't ask for a more welcome guest," said Bilíbin, coming out to meet Prince Andrew. "Franz, put the prince's things in my bedroom," he told the servant who was showing Bolkónski in. "So you're a bearer of victory news? Wonderful! And here I am sitting around sick, as you can see."
After washing and changing, Prince Andrew came into the diplomat's luxurious study and sat down to the dinner that had been prepared for him. Bilíbin settled himself comfortably by the fire.

After his journey and the campaign, during which he'd been deprived of every comfort of cleanliness and refinement, Prince Andrew felt a pleasant sense of ease among the luxurious surroundings he'd been accustomed to since childhood. Beyond that, it was pleasant—after his reception by the Austrians—to speak, if not in Russian (they were speaking French), at least with a Russian who would, he assumed, share the general Russian hostility toward the Austrians that was particularly intense at the time.

Bilíbin was a thirty-five-year-old bachelor who moved in the same circles as Prince Andrew. They'd known each other previously in Petersburg but had become closer when Prince Andrew was in Vienna with Kutúzov. Just as Prince Andrew was a young man who showed every sign of rising high in the military, so Bilíbin—to an even greater extent—showed every sign of rising in the diplomatic world. He was still young but no longer a novice diplomat, having entered the service at sixteen and served in Paris and Copenhagen before landing a fairly important post in Vienna. Both the foreign minister and the Russian ambassador in Vienna knew him and valued him. He wasn't one of those many diplomats who are respected merely because they have certain negative qualities, avoid doing certain things, and speak French. He was one of those who genuinely enjoyed work and knew how to do it well, and despite his natural laziness would sometimes spend an entire night at his desk. He worked well regardless of the subject matter. It wasn't the question "What for?" but "How?" that interested him. He didn't particularly care what a diplomatic matter was about, but it gave him enormous pleasure to craft a circular, memorandum, or report with skill, precision, and elegance. Bilíbin's services were valued not only for his writing but also for his ability to deal and converse with people in the highest spheres.

Bilíbin enjoyed conversation the way he enjoyed work—only when it could be made elegantly witty. In society he was always waiting for a chance to say something memorable and only joined a conversation when such an opportunity arose. His talk was always laced with cleverly original, polished phrases of general interest. These sayings were prepared in the inner workshop of his mind in portable form, as if designed so that minor society figures could carry them from one drawing room to the next. And indeed, Bilíbin's witticisms circulated through the Viennese salons and often had an influence on matters considered important.

His thin, worn, sallow face was covered with deep wrinkles that always looked as clean and well-scrubbed as fingertips after a long bath. The movement of these wrinkles was the principal means of expression on his face. His forehead would furrow into deep folds with his eyebrows raised, then his eyebrows would drop and deep creases would form on his cheeks. His small, deep-set eyes always sparkled and looked straight at you.
"Well, tell me about your exploits," he said.
Bolkónski, very modestly and without once mentioning himself, described the battle and his reception by the Minister of War.
"They received me and my news the way you'd receive a dog that wanders into a bowling alley," he concluded.
Bilíbin smiled and the wrinkles on his face disappeared.

“Cependant, mon cher,” he remarked, examining his nails from a distance and puckering the skin above his left eye, “malgré la haute estime que je professe pour the Orthodox Russian army, j’avoue que votre victoire n’est pas des plus victorieuses.” *
* “But my dear fellow, with all my respect for the Orthodox Russian army, I must say that your victory was not particularly victorious.”
He went on talking this way in French, switching to Russian only for words he wanted to make contemptuous.
"Come now! You fell on the unfortunate Mortier with your entire force—his single division—and even then Mortier slipped through your fingers! Where's the victory in that?"
"But seriously," said Prince Andrew, "we can at least say without boasting that it was somewhat better than Ulm..."
"Why didn't you capture even one marshal for us?"

"Because things don't always go according to plan or unfold with parade-ground precision. We expected, as I told you, to reach their rear by seven in the morning but didn't get there until five in the afternoon."
"And why didn't you get there at seven in the morning? You should have been there by seven," returned Bilíbin with a smile. "You should have been there at seven in the morning."
"Why didn't you manage to convince Bonaparte through diplomatic channels to leave Genoa alone?" retorted Prince Andrew in the same tone.

"I know," interrupted Bilíbin, "you're thinking it's very easy to capture marshals while sitting on a sofa by the fire! That's true enough, but still—why didn't you capture him? So don't be surprised if not only the Minister of War but also His Most August Majesty Emperor and King Francis isn't exactly thrilled by your victory. Even I, a lowly secretary of the Russian Embassy, feel no need to celebrate by giving my Franz a coin or letting him go off to the Prater with his sweetheart... Though of course, we don't have a Prater here."
He looked Prince Andrew straight in the eye and suddenly smoothed his forehead.

"Now it's my turn to ask you 'why?' my dear fellow," said Bolkónski. "I confess I don't understand—perhaps there are diplomatic subtleties here beyond my humble intelligence—but I can't make sense of it. Mack loses an entire army, Archduke Ferdinand and Archduke Karl show no signs of life and blunder after blunder. Kutúzov alone wins a real victory, breaking the spell of French invincibility, and the Minister of War doesn't even want to hear the details."

"That's exactly the point, my dear fellow. You see, it's all 'hurrah for the Tsar, for Russia, for the Orthodox faith!' That's all very well, but what do we—I mean the Austrian court—care about your victories? Bring us good news of a victory by Archduke Karl or Ferdinand—one archduke's as good as another, as you know—even if it's only over a fire brigade of Bonaparte's, and that would be another story entirely: we'd fire off cannons! But this kind of thing seems designed to annoy us. Archduke Karl does nothing, Archduke Ferdinand disgraces himself. You abandon Vienna, give up its defense—as if to say: 'God is with us, but you and your capital are on your own!' The one general we all loved—Schmidt—you get killed by a bullet, and then you congratulate us on the victory! Admit it: more irritating news than yours could hardly be imagined. It's as though it were done on purpose, completely on purpose. Besides, suppose you did win a brilliant victory—even if Archduke Karl had won one—what difference would it make to the overall course of events? It's too late now that Vienna is occupied by the French army!"
"What? Occupied? Vienna occupied?"
"Not only occupied—Bonaparte is at Schönbrunn, and the count, our dear Count Vrbna, goes to him for his orders."
After the exhaustion of the journey, his reception, and especially after dinner, Bolkónski found he could not fully grasp the significance of what he was hearing.

"Count Lichtenfels was here this morning," Bilíbin continued, "and showed me a letter describing the French parade through Vienna in full detail: Prince Murat and the whole spectacle... So you see, your victory is hardly cause for celebration, and you can't expect to be received as a savior."

"Honestly, I don't care about that. I really don't care at all," said Prince Andrew, beginning to realize that his news of the battle near Krems was truly insignificant compared to something like the fall of Austria's capital. "But how was Vienna taken? What about the bridge and its famous fortifications? What about Prince Auersperg? We'd heard that Prince Auersperg was defending Vienna."

"Prince Auersperg is on this side of the river—our side—and he's defending us. Doing it rather badly, I'd say, but still defending us. Vienna, though, is on the other side. No, the bridge hasn't been taken yet, and I hope it won't be, since it's been mined and orders have been given to blow it up. Otherwise we'd have long since been in the Bohemian mountains, and you and your army would have had a very bad time caught between two fires."
"But this still doesn't mean the campaign is over," said Prince Andrew.

"Well, I think it is. The big men here think so too, but they don't dare say it. It will be as I said at the start of the campaign: it won't be your skirmish at Dürrenstein, or gunpowder at all, that decides this—but the people who planned it," said Bilíbin, quoting one of his own bon mots, releasing the wrinkles on his forehead, and pausing. "The only question now is what comes of the meeting between Emperor Alexander and the King of Prussia in Berlin. If Prussia joins the allies, Austria's hand will be forced and there will be war. If not, it's just a matter of deciding where to draw up the terms of the new Campo Formio."
"What an extraordinary genius!" Prince Andrew suddenly exclaimed, clenching his small fist and striking the table. "And what luck the man has!"

"Bonaparte?" said Bilíbin inquiringly, wrinkling his forehead to signal that a witticism was coming. "Buonaparte?" he repeated, stressing the 'u.' "I think, however, now that he's laying down the law for Austria at Schönbrunn, we really must drop the 'u.' I shall certainly adopt the innovation and simply call him Bonaparte!"
[Bilíbin's joke: "We must let him off the 'u'!" — a pun on the French spelling of Buonaparte vs. Bonaparte.]
"But joking aside," said Prince Andrew, "do you really think the campaign is over?"

"Here's what I think. Austria has been made a fool of, and she's not used to it. She'll retaliate. And she's been made a fool of in the first place because her provinces have been pillaged—they say the holy Russian army loots terribly—her army is destroyed, her capital taken, and all this for the sake of His Sardinian Majesty's lovely eyes. And therefore—this is just between us—I have an instinctive feeling that we're being deceived. My instinct tells me there are negotiations with France going on, and plans for peace—a secret, separate peace."
["Lovely eyes" — from the French expression "beaux yeux," meaning for someone's sake, implying an unworthy cause.]
"Impossible!" cried Prince Andrew. "That would be too despicable."
"If we live, we'll see," replied Bilíbin, his face becoming smooth again—a sign the conversation was over.

When Prince Andrew reached the room prepared for him and lay down in a clean shirt on the feather bed with its warm, fragrant pillows, he felt that the battle whose news he'd brought was far, far away from him. The alliance with Prussia, Austria's treachery, Bonaparte's latest triumph, tomorrow's levee and parade, and his audience with Emperor Francis occupied his thoughts.

He closed his eyes, and immediately a roar of cannon fire, musketry, and the rattling of carriage wheels seemed to fill his ears, and once again in his mind the musketeers were descending the hill in a thin line, the French were firing, and he felt his heart pounding as he rode forward beside Schmidt with bullets whistling cheerfully all around. He experienced the joy of being alive tenfold, as he hadn't since childhood.
He woke up...
"Yes, all of that really happened!" he said, and smiling to himself like a happy child, he fell into a deep, youthful sleep.
